# Voice profile — eff-mullin

## 1. Cadence

Two interruption habits define the rhythm of this prose. The first is the parenthetical span. The measure — [measurement:round-parenthetical-spans] Count each non-nested pair of round brackets whose contents stay on one line in the extracted sample bodies — finds 97 pairs across all 11 samples, 12.03 per 1,000 words, throughout. These parentheses carry citations, brief definitions, or qualifications mid-sentence without stalling the main clause. The second is the em-dash: [measurement:em-dashes] Count every literal em-dash character in the extracted sample bodies — 53 instances across 10/11 samples, 6.57 per 1,000 words, throughout in pieces that use them. Em-dashes mark the moment when a consequence or contradiction needs to land harder than a parenthesis allows.

Against this dense mid-sentence interruption, short declarative sentences appear several times per piece in 9/11 samples, closing a paragraph that has loaded and discharged its qualifications. `court-records`: *"Public access to the courts is a cornerstone of democratic accountability."* `kids-online-safety`: *"When the safest legal option is to delete a forum, platforms will delete the forum."* The pattern: build the argument in medium-length interrupted sentences; close the section in ten words or fewer. If the paragraph has run long and parliamentary, the last sentence cuts short.

## 2. How a piece opens

Nine of eleven pieces open by naming the bill or policy subject in the first sentence, placing the reader immediately inside the legislative debate. The form is a noun phrase identifying the legislation followed by a brief characterising clause: *"A.B. 412, the flawed California bill that threatened small developers in the name of AI 'transparency,' has been delayed"* (`california-ab-412-stalls`); *"The Kids Online Safety Act (KOSA) is back in the Senate"* (`kids-online-safety`). Two pieces open with a dateline update notice before the body proper; treat that frame as separate from the opening proper.

No opening pauses to establish why the topic matters — that is assumed. Put the bill name, the vote, or the named threat in sentence one.

## 3. How a piece closes

Nine of eleven pieces end with a direct verdict, an explicit call to legislative action, or both. The move is: name the body that should act, state what it should do, stop. `congress-just-rushed`: *"The Senate should reject H.R. 6028. The Copyright Office should serve the public—not presidential administrations, and not industry lobbyists."* `kids-online-safety`: *"Lawmakers should reject it, and fast."* The final sentence is rarely the longest in the paragraph. Close short.

## 4. Who is being addressed, and how

The argument is carried by an institutional "we" representing EFF. [measurement:first-person-plural-family] Count case-sensitive whole-word tokens we, We, us, our, Our, ours, Ours, and the listed contracted we forms in the extracted sample bodies; uppercase US is excluded — 19 instances across 10/11 samples, 2.36 per 1,000 words, once or twice per piece. This is not an inclusive "we" recruiting the reader; it marks EFF's positions and actions: *"We told them changes to the Copyright Office will have major consequences"* (`congress-just-rushed`). The reader is addressed as an informed observer, not pulled into the collective.

First-person singular is near-absent. [measurement:first-person-singular-family] Count case-insensitive whole-word tokens I, me, my, mine, and myself in the extracted sample bodies — 2 instances across 2/11 samples only, 0.25 per 1,000 words. The author does not appear as an individual with history or opinion independent of EFF. Do not use "I."

Second-person address is sparse: [measurement:second-person-family] Count case-insensitive whole-word tokens you, your, yours, you're, you've, you'd, and you'll in the extracted sample bodies — 11 instances in 5/11 samples, 1.36 per 1,000 words. When it appears, it is almost exclusively at piece-ends inviting California residents to contact legislators — functional and specific, not conversational.

Contractions run throughout all 11 samples. [measurement:contractions] Count whole-word n't, 're, 've, 'll, 'd, and 'm forms plus 's only for the closed elision hosts it, that, there, here, who, what, where, when, how, why, he, she, let, one, nothing, everything, something, somebody, nobody, and this; possessive 's is excluded — 86 instances, 10.66 per 1,000 words. The prose is informal in this sense: *"it's," "won't," "that's"* appear freely. Against them, uncontracted negatives — [measurement:uncontracted-negatives] Count case-insensitive whole phrases do not, does not, did not, is not, are not, was not, were not, cannot, could not, would not, should not, will not, have not, has not, and had not in the extracted sample bodies — total 32 instances across 9/11 samples, 3.97 per 1,000 words, once or twice per piece on average. Uncontracted forms appear when the stress falls on the negation itself: *"That is not a new issue for EFF"* (`court-records`).

No profanity or vulgarity appears: [measurement:profanity-vulgarity] Count only the case-insensitive whole-word profanity and vulgarity forms enumerated by the prose-author corpus-rates profanity rule; coined words containing a rude root are excluded — 0 instances across all 11 samples. Informal register comes from contractions and directness, never from coarseness.

Rhetorical questions appear in 4/11 samples, several times per piece when present. [measurement:question-marks] Count every literal question-mark character in the extracted sample bodies — 9 instances, 1.12 per 1,000 words. These are diagnostic, not genuine inquiry: *"Why Are Gay Bars Building Databases of Their Patrons?"* (`why-are-gay-bars`).

Named opponents appear in 10/11 samples — specific bills, agencies, and companies called by name — and named allies and sources appear alongside them, several times per piece. Courts, coalition letters, and named organisations supply authority; abstract principle alone does not carry the argument.

## 5. Figures

Figures appear several times per piece in 7/11 samples, drawn from the vocabulary of law, bureaucracy, and the market: *"cumbersome beast"* (the copyright registration system, `californias-ab-412-bill`), *"death sentence"* for startups (`californias-ab-412-bill`), *"smokescreen"* (`kids-online-safety`), *"heckler's veto"* (`congress-narrowed-guard`), *"sleight-of-hand"* (`kids-online-safety`). A figure runs one clause and is never reopened. No extended analogy develops across a paragraph.

No rate is given because the boundary of a figure cannot be drawn consistently enough for a second counter to reproduce the number. The vocabulary figures are built from is legal and bureaucratic English; use it at roughly the corpus density — one image per section at most.

## 6. Register range

All eleven pieces argue against a named legislative or regulatory threat. The register does not shift. Longer pieces use bold prose subheadings — 8/11 samples (`chatbot-act`: *"The CHATBOT Act Creates New Privacy Risks For Families"*) — as the primary pacing instrument, naming each section's next claim before a new paragraph begins. Shorter pieces run in continuous paragraphs. Length changes; tone does not.

## 7. What the corpus never does

Structure is carried through bold prose subheadings — 8/11 samples — not through bullet lists or numbered enumerations. Nothing in the corpus uses a bullet point or ordered list to present an argument; 11/11 samples. A subheading does the work bullets would elsewhere: write a short phrase naming the section's claim, bold it, start a new paragraph.

## 8. What this profile could not determine

**Voice card:** Empty. Every observation is derived from the corpus alone.

**Qualification and hedging:** Modal hedging (*"may," "could," "will likely"*) appears, but not at a rate that settles into a drafter-usable pattern. The dominant mode is direct assertion. Unresolved.

**Typographic note:** All eleven sources are published blog posts rendered by a CMS. Em-dash and parenthesis counts reflect the published page and could involve editorial formatting. These are treated as authorial on the assumption that advocacy blog posts of this type are author-controlled, but a drafter should note the caveat. The same applies to bold subheadings.

**Four observations were dropped** for insufficient citation: a "Bottom line:" summary formula (1/11 only), a rhetorical inversion pattern (*"not X — Y"*), a paragraph structure of concession-before-rebuttal, and a habit of opening with the bill's stated purpose before rebutting it. Each appeared plausible on reading but could not be cited consistently across two or more samples.
